File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018") or SHA1 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018") or MD5 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018") or SHA1 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018") or MD5 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

        where Processes.process_hash IN ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process_hash

iCagenda and Balbooa Forms Joomla Flaws Reportedly Exploited as Zero-Days

The Hacker News
2026-07-13 4 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added two maximum-severity security flaws impacting iCagenda and Balbooa extensions for Joomla to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, following reports of zero-day exploitation in the wild. The vulnerabilities, both rated 10.0 on the CVSS scoring system, are below - CVE-2026-48939 - A vulnerability in the

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] iCagenda 'Submit an Event' scanner UA 'icagenda-batch/1.0' in web logs (CVE-2026-48939)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] PHP web shell written to Joomla iCagenda/Balbooa upload folders (CVE-2026-48939, CVE-2026-56291)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] HTTP request to planted PHP shell under iCagenda/Balbooa upload paths (CVE-2026-48939, CVE-2026-56291)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
iCagenda 'Submit an Event' scanner UA 'icagenda-batch/1.0' in web logs (CVE-2026-48939) AIDelivery High
Hunts web-server access logs for the automated exploitation scanner that identifies itself with the User-Agent 'icagenda-batch/1.0', the exact tool mySites.guru observed grabbing a token and POSTing a malicious upload to the iCagenda Submit-an-Event endpoint since 15 June 2026. This UA is not a legitimate browser, crawler or monitoring agent, so any hit is a direct exploitation attempt against CVE-2026-48939. Rationale: Uses the literal exploitation scanner UA 'icagenda-batch/1.0' named by mySites.guru and reproduced in the article; a non-browser UA string this specific has effectively zero legitimate use, making it alerting-grade on the first hit. Cross-checked against: • https://mysites.guru/blog/icagenda-zero-day-file-upload-rce/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-warns-of-actively-exploited-rce-flaws-in-joomla-extensions/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4rh3-rmh3-hv6h
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) deliberately fingerprinting iCagenda with a spoofed UA during an authorized scan
  • Security researcher / red-team replaying the PoC against a staging site
  • A monitoring probe an admin scripted using the same UA string to test their own patch
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the matched source IP(s) — confirm the sequence token GET -> POST to the iCagenda submit endpoint -> GET of a new .php under images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge and, if a PHP file was fetched, take the site offline or WAF-block the attachments path immediately. 3) Hunt: list images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/ for any .php/.phtml files, diff the Joomla #__users table for new Super Admin accounts, and confirm iCagenda is on 4.0.8/3.9.15.

PHP web shell written to Joomla iCagenda/Balbooa upload folders (CVE-2026-48939, CVE-2026-56291) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of a PHP-executable file inside the two upload directories these flaws write to — 'images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/' and 'images/baforms/uploads' — which by design should only ever hold user-submitted images and documents. A .php/.phtml/.phar in either folder is the planted web shell mySites.guru flagged as the primary IOC for both CVEs. Rationale: Pins on the two exact upload paths (images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/, images/baforms/uploads) plus PHP-executable extensions — both vendors explicitly say these folders must never contain PHP, so any hit is the planted shell rather than a legit attachment. Cross-checked against: • https://mysites.guru/blog/icagenda-zero-day-file-upload-rce/ • https://mysites.guru/blog/balbooa-forms-unauthenticated-file-upload-flaw/ • https://www.cycognito.com/blog/emerging-threat-cve-2026-56291-balbooa-forms-remote-code-execution-via-unauthenticated-file-upload/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Site migration/backup-restore tooling (Akeeba Kickstart, rsync) copying the whole webroot including an already-present benign file that happens to match
  • Admin manually placing a legitimate index.php as a directory-listing guard in the uploads folder
  • A previous compromise remediation that quarantined-in-place rather than deleting, retriggering on file rename
  • Antivirus renaming a detected file to .php.quarantine style names
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("kickstart.php","restore.php") and not (FolderPath has "backup" or FolderPath has "tmp\\install")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the dropped file — decode any eval/base64/assert/system calls, note the SHA256 and the InitiatingProcess (should be the web server / php-fpm). 2) Contain: delete/quarantine the file, WAF-block direct requests to the two upload paths, and isolate the host if the shell was already accessed. 3) Hunt: pull web logs for GET requests to that filename (attacker interaction), search for new Joomla Super Admin accounts and other recently-modified PHP files across the webroot, and confirm iCagenda>=4.0.8/3.9.15 and Balbooa Forms>=2.4.1.
DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed") | where FileName has_any (".php",".phtml",".phar",".php5") | where (FolderPath has "icagenda" and FolderPath has "attachments") or (FolderPath has "baforms" and FolderPath has "uploads") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256 | order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where TargetFileName has_any (".php",".phtml",".phar",".php5") | where (TargetFilePath has "icagenda" and TargetFilePath has "attachments") or (TargetFilePath has "baforms" and TargetFilePath has "uploads") | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername, TargetFileSHA256 | sort by TimeGenerated desc

HTTP request to planted PHP shell under iCagenda/Balbooa upload paths (CVE-2026-48939, CVE-2026-56291) AICommand & Control High
Detects the attacker fetching/executing the planted web shell — a GET/POST to a .php file located under 'images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/' or 'images/baforms/uploads' in web-server access logs. mySites.guru observed the scanner 'fetched the planted shell at the exact path the component writes attachments to', and requests to a PHP file in a media-upload directory are inherently anomalous. Rationale: Combines the two literal upload URI paths from both advisories with a '.php' request — a PHP file being requested from a media-attachment directory is the web-shell-interaction signal, distinct from the file-drop and the scanner-UA pivots. Cross-checked against: • https://mysites.guru/blog/icagenda-zero-day-file-upload-rce/ • https://mysites.guru/blog/balbooa-forms-unauthenticated-file-upload-flaw/ • https://www.securityweek.com/organizations-warned-of-exploited-joomla-extension-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate index.php directory-index guard in the uploads folder being requested by a crawler
  • Internal DAST/WAF validation scan probing the patched path and receiving a 404 (filter on scStatus==200 to cut these)
  • Uptime monitor configured to hit a known-good health-check PHP under a media path
Suppression filter
| where Status == 200
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the response status — a 200 to a .php in these folders means the shell executed; capture the source IP, requested filename and any query-string commands. 2) Contain: block the source IP and the upload path at the WAF, then delete the referenced PHP file from disk and isolate the web host. 3) Hunt: correlate the filename back to the DeviceFileEvents/FileWritten drop, review Joomla admin-user changes and outbound connections from the web host in the same window, and verify both extensions are patched.
union isfuzzy=true (W3CIISLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | project TimeGenerated, Src=cIP, Host=Computer, Method=csMethod, Uri=csUriStem, Status=scStatus, UA=csUserAgent), (AppServiceHTTPLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | project TimeGenerated, Src=CIp, Host=CsHost, Method=CsMethod, Uri=CsUriStem, Status=ScStatus, UA=UserAgent) | where (Uri has "/images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/" or Uri has "/images/baforms/uploads/") and Uri has ".php" | sort by TimeGenerated desc

jscrambler npm package publishes malicious preinstall binary

StepSecurity
2026-07-12 15 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On July 11, 2026, version 8.14.0 of jscrambler was published to npm carrying a malicious preinstall hook that drops and executes a platform-specific native binary on Linux, Windows, and macOS. jscrambler is the official CLI client for the Jscrambler Code Integrity API, a commercial JavaScript obfuscation and web-app protection service, with a clean version history dating back to 0.1.0. The compromised release was flagged by StepSecurity's AI Release Analyzer with a suspicion score of 0 (the maximum suspicion rating) on publish.

Compromised jscrambler npm package (8.14.0+) artifacts written to node_modules AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for on-disk artifacts of the trojanized jscrambler npm release: the 7.8 MB dist/intro.js binary container written under node_modules/jscrambler and the extracted per-platform stealer payload hashes. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact package path, the disguised container file, and the three published payload SHA256s. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact IOC matrix: node_modules/jscrambler/dist/intro.js and the three extracted payload SHA256s. Corroborated by Socket.dev and The Hacker News, which confirmed the same package/path and Rust-compiled cross-platform stealer. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://www.mallory.ai/stories/019f5225-a834-719b-9b66-c82edd147d7c

npm/node preinstall drops and executes hidden native binary from OS temp dir AIInstallation High
Hunts the core execution step: the jscrambler preinstall loader (dist/setup.js) decompresses a platform binary to a randomly named dotfile in the OS temp directory and launches it detached from the npm install tree. Detects node/npm spawning an executable whose path is a hidden dotfile under Temp or /tmp. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's loader behaviour: preinstall reads dist/intro.js and spawns a randomly named dotfile in the OS temp dir (.[a-z0-9]{6,} with .exe on Windows) detached from npm. Parent=node/npm + hidden temp binary is extremely rare in benign builds. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1204.003 T1036.008
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit native postinstall tools (esbuild, node-sass, sharp) extracting prebuilt binaries to temp — but those are not hidden dotfiles
  • node-based test harnesses that shell out to a scratch temp binary
  • Electron/pkg self-extracting apps unpacking to temp on first run
  • Yarn/pnpm build steps writing temp helper executables (rarely dotfiles)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("esbuild","node-sass","node-gyp","sharp","electron-builder"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the temp file path and SHA256, confirm parent is node/npm during an install window, and check if jscrambler 8.14.0+ is present. 2) Contain: kill the detached temp process, quarantine the temp binary, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pull the process's outbound connections (Tor/C2 IPs), look for browser credential-store and .npmrc file access, and enumerate other hosts that installed the same package version.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","node")
| where FolderPath has_any ("Temp","/tmp/")
| where FileName startswith "."
| where FileName endswith ".exe" or FolderPath has "/tmp/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| where NewProcessName has "Temp"
| extend LeafName = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where LeafName startswith "." and LeafName endswith ".exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Execution of extracted jscrambler stealer payload by SHA256 AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on any process launched from one of the three published, extracted stealer payloads (ELF/PE32+/Mach-O) regardless of file name or drop path, catching the payload even if the loader randomizes its temp filename. Rationale: Uses the three exact payload SHA256s from the IOC table; hash-based execution detection survives the loader's random temp filename and is near-zero FP. Second-sourced as a Rust cross-platform infostealer by The Hacker News/Socket. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html

Stealer C2 egress to Tor Project infrastructure and hardcoded IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound connections from a developer/CI host to the two hardcoded stealer C2 IPs and the check/archive.torproject.org endpoints the dropped binary contacts. High-fidelity because these are specific attacker-tied indicators, not generic Tor usage. Rationale: Uses the exact C2 IPs (37.27.122.124, 57.128.246.79) and torproject.org endpoints named in the Harden-Runner analysis and independently confirmed by second sources. Any dev host reaching these is high-signal for the stealer's C2. npm/node install spawns reconnaissance or shell utilities AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the preinstall execution phase where the compromised package's install context spawns local shells or host-recon tools — deviation from normal build behaviour. Reviewer-requested; grounded in the article's automatic preinstall-hook execution during npm install. Rationale: The article confirms the malicious code runs automatically via the npm preinstall hook; recon/download tools spawned by node/npm during install are anomalous for a JS-obfuscation CLI build and map to the stealer's discovery/staging behaviour reported by second sources (env/.npmrc/cloud-cred collection). Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1087 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI/CD build scripts that legitimately call curl/wget to fetch assets during install
  • node-based tooling invoking net.exe/reg.exe for environment setup
  • postinstall scripts running hostname/ipconfig for telemetry
  • cross-platform build tools shelling out to sh/uname on Linux runners
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild-install","electron","cypress","playwright install")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the parent npm/node command line and the package being installed; confirm whether jscrambler 8.14.0+ (or another unexpected package) is in the tree. 2) Contain: if unexpected, isolate the host and halt the CI job. 3) Hunt: pivot to any hidden temp binary spawned by the same node process, C2 egress, and access to .npmrc / browser credential stores.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","node","npm")
| where FileName in~ ("whoami.exe","systeminfo.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","hostname.exe","ipconfig.exe","reg.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","whoami","hostname","id","uname","curl","wget")
| summarize ChildCount = dcount(FileName), Children = make_set(FileName), SampleCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where ChildCount >= 1
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| extend Child = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where Child in~ ("whoami.exe","systeminfo.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","hostname.exe","ipconfig.exe","reg.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| summarize ChildCount = dcount(Child), Children = make_set(Child) by Computer, SubjectUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where ChildCount >= 1
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: npm/node install spawns recon or shell utility
id: c1d8e4b2-9a37-4f6c-8b1d-3e7a2c0f9d61
description: Detects node/npm spawning host-reconnaissance or download utilities during package installation, matching malicious preinstall behaviour
references:

tags:

detection:

  condition: selection

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\node.exe OR *\\npm.exe) @Image:(*\\whoami.exe OR *\\systeminfo.exe OR *\\net.exe OR *\\net1.exe OR *\\hostname.exe OR *\\ipconfig.exe OR *\\reg.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\wget.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(node|npm)\.exe$/i

| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Processes.process_name) as children from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","npm.exe","node","npm") AND Processes.process_name IN ("whoami.exe","systeminfo.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","hostname.exe","ipconfig.exe","reg.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","whoami","hostname","id","uname","curl","wget") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where mvcount(children) >= 1 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process_name) as children from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","npm.exe","node","npm") AND Processes.process_name IN ("whoami.exe","systeminfo.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","hostname.exe","ipconfig.exe","reg.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","whoami","hostname","id","uname","curl","wget") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where mvcount(children) >= 1 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Persistence created by hidden temp-dir binary (scheduled task / Run key) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the stealer establishing persistence: a hidden binary running from the OS temp directory spawning schtasks.exe or writing a Run-key/registry autostart. Grounded in the article's temp-dotfile drop and corroborated persistence (Windows scheduled task / macOS LaunchAgent) reported by second sources. Rationale: Chains the article's temp-dotfile binary (from the IOC table) to the persistence step confirmed by second sources (Windows scheduled task / macOS LaunchAgent). Parent = hidden temp binary spawning schtasks/reg is a rare, high-fidelity persistence pivot distinct from the drop/exec UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate temp-extracted installer registering a scheduled task on first run
  • Software updaters writing a Run key from a temp staging binary
  • Admin scripting that creates scheduled tasks from a temp-located tool
  • EDR/RMM agents bootstrapping persistence from a temp path
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has_any ("Packages","WindowsApps","Program Files")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the scheduled-task/Run-key target and the parent temp binary hash; confirm parent is a hidden dotfile. 2) Contain: delete the persistence entry, quarantine the temp binary, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: check for the payload SHA256, C2 egress to the known IPs/Tor domains, and jscrambler 8.14.0+ across the fleet; on macOS look for a matching LaunchAgent plist.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "Temp"
| extend ParentLeaf = tostring(split(InitiatingProcessFolderPath, "\\")[-1])
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "."
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/create")
   or (FileName =~ "reg.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "Run")
   or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("New-ScheduledTask","CurrentVersion\\Run"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has "Temp"
| extend ParentLeaf = tostring(split(ParentProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where ParentLeaf startswith "."
| extend Child = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where (Child =~ "schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "/create")
   or (Child =~ "reg.exe" and CommandLine has "Run")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Hidden temp-dir binary establishes persistence via schtasks or Run key
id: a5f2c8d1-7b40-4e93-9c6a-2d1b8e0f4a72
description: Detects a hidden dotfile binary in the OS temp directory spawning schtasks /create or writing a registry Run key, matching jscrambler stealer persistence
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/14

  - attack.t1547.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|contains: '\Temp\.'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\schtasks.exe'
      - '\reg.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/create'
      - '\Run'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\Temp\\.*.exe) @Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\reg.exe) @CommandLine:(*create* OR *Run*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentImageFileName=/[\/\\]\.[a-z0-9]{6,}(\.exe)?$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(schtasks|reg)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/(\/create|\\Run)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentImageFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_path="*\\Temp\\.*" AND Processes.process_name IN ("schtasks.exe","reg.exe","powershell.exe") AND (Processes.process="*create*" OR Processes.process="*\\Run*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_path Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_path="*\\Temp\\.*" AND Processes.process_name IN ("schtasks.exe","reg.exe","powershell.exe") AND (Processes.process="*create*" OR Processes.process="*\\Run*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_path Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Compromised jscrambler 8.14.0 npm Release Drops Rust Infostealer During Install

The Hacker News
2026-07-11 14 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The jscrambler npm package was compromised, and simply installing its&nbsp;8.14.0&nbsp;release runs an infostealer on your machine. jscrambler 8.14.0 npm Package Installation AIDelivery High
Hunts for installation of the compromised jscrambler CLI npm package (8.14.0 and the sibling malicious versions 8.16.0/8.17.0/8.18.0/8.20.0 tied to the same actor) via npm/pnpm/yarn command lines on developer and CI hosts. Article-specific because it pins the exact package name and poisoned version window rather than generic npm abuse. Rationale: Anchors on the exact package name 'jscrambler' plus the poisoned version set from the article (8.14.0) enriched with the sibling malicious versions Socket attributed to the same actor. Version-pinned package name in an install command is very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-backdoor-jscrambler-npm-package-with-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A dependency-audit or SCA tool that echoes 'jscrambler@8.14.0' in its scan output command line
  • A remediation script explicitly uninstalling/overriding jscrambler@8.14.0 (npm uninstall / npm ls output)
  • A CI lockfile-pinning job that references the version string while forcing an upgrade to 8.15.0
  • A developer reproducing the incident in an isolated sandbox
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("uninstall","npm ls","npm audit","remove"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the command was an install (npm install/ci/add) not an uninstall/audit, and check whether the host is a build agent or developer laptop with access to cloud keys. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any node.exe child processes, and remove jscrambler@8.14.0 from lockfiles/caches; pin to 8.13.0 or 8.15.0. 3) Hunt: on any confirmed install, treat all reachable secrets as stolen — rotate AWS/Azure/GCP keys, npm/GitHub tokens, and AI-tool/MCP API keys; pivot to UC2/UC3 to find the dropped binary and C2 callbacks.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe") or FileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "jscrambler" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("8.14.0","8.16.0","8.17.0","8.18.0","8.20.0")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "jscrambler" and CommandLine has_any ("8.14.0","8.16.0","8.17.0","8.18.0","8.20.0")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rust Infostealer Binary Execution from npm Post-Install Hook AIInstallation High
Detects the setup.js preinstall loader (run by node.exe/npm) writing a hidden, randomly-named native binary into the system temp directory and executing it detached. Matches on the three published payload hashes and on the node→temp-hidden-executable parent/child chain specific to this campaign. Rationale: Uses the three published decompressed payload SHA-256 values plus the article's described chain (setup.js under node writes a hidden .{random}/.{random}.exe into temp and launches it detached). Hash match is deterministic; the behavioral clause catches recompiled variants. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-backdoor-jscrambler-npm-package-with-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate node-gyp / native-addon builds that write and run compiled binaries from temp during install
  • Electron or Puppeteer post-install steps that unpack helper binaries into temp
  • Test frameworks that spawn short-lived helper executables from a temp workspace
  • A developer's own build tool that emits dot-prefixed cache files in temp
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild","electron-builder") and SHA256 !in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd","b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903","c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: if a hash matches, this is confirmed malware — no further validation needed; for the behavioral hit, inspect the temp file name/signature and whether it was launched detached with hidden output. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the temp process tree, and capture the binary for the DFIR queue before AV quarantine removes it. 3) Hunt: pivot on the process ID into UC3 (C2 to 37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79), UC4 (credential file access), and UC5 (persistence) on the same host and across all CI agents that pulled jscrambler in the July 11+ window.

   or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe") and FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/") and FileName startswith ".")

IronWorm C2 beacon to hardcoded jscrambler stealer IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any host reaching the two hard-coded attacker C2 IP addresses (37.27.122.124, 57.128.246.79) that StepSecurity observed the dropped jscrambler stealer contacting over TLS. Pure network-IOC pivot; independent of process telemetry so it catches the stealer even if EDR missed the drop. Rationale: Uses the two direct attacker C2 IPs StepSecurity published — the first network indicators for the campaign, confirmed across multiple write-ups. Static malicious IPs have essentially no legitimate business use. cloudwatch_query left empty: this is endpoint/firewall egress telemetry that does not live in CloudTrail, and VPC Flow fields fall outside the CloudTrail whitelist. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-backdoor-jscrambler-npm-package-with-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel enrichment or sandbox appliance deliberately connecting to the IOC IPs for analysis
  • A security researcher detonating the sample in a lab that shares the corporate egress
  • Shared cloud-provider IP reuse if the attacker infra is later reassigned (Hetzner/OVH ranges)
  • A vulnerability scanner probing the IPs as part of external attack-surface testing
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-lab","detonation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the host — if it maps to a temp-dropped hidden binary or node.exe child, escalate to confirmed stealer C2. 2) Contain: block 37.27.122.124 and 57.128.246.79 at the perimeter/EDR, isolate the source host, and snapshot memory. 3) Hunt: sweep all egress logs for these IPs and Tor bootstrap traffic (check.torproject.org / archive.torproject.org) from build agents; correlate to UC1 installs and rotate every secret reachable from that host.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("37.27.122.124","57.128.246.79")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Credential/Browser Data Theft Post-npm Install AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a hidden temp-directory process (the dropped Rust stealer) touching the specific secret stores the article enumerates: AWS/Azure/GCP credentials, .ssh keys, Chrome/Edge user data, Bitwarden/MetaMask/Exodus/Phantom wallets, and AI-coding-tool configs (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, VS Code, Zed) that hold API keys and MCP credentials. Rationale: Pairs the article's exact target list (AWS/Azure/GCP, .ssh, Chrome/Edge, Bitwarden, MetaMask/Exodus/Phantom, and the newer AI-tool configs for Claude/Cursor/Windsurf/VS Code/Zed) with the initiating process being the hidden temp-dropped binary — the two together are far more specific than any single credential-store access. datadog_query empty: Sysmon does not emit reliable file-read events (EID 11 is create-only), so this read-centric detection cannot be faithfully expressed on Datadog Windows telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1552.001 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate backup or sync agent running from a temp workspace enumerating user profile directories
  • AWS/Azure/gcloud CLI credential refresh reading ~/.aws or ~/.azure
  • A browser or password-manager updater accessing its own User Data directory
  • A legitimate AI coding assistant (Cursor/Windsurf) reading its own config from an installer staged in temp
  • Endpoint AV scanning the same secret directories
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("aws.exe","az.exe","gcloud","bitwarden","chrome.exe","msedge.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files", "/usr/bin/", "/opt/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the acting process is the hidden temp binary (dot-prefixed, random name) and not a signed vendor updater; check how many distinct secret stores it touched in the window. 2) Contain: isolate the host and preserve the binary; assume every accessed store is compromised. 3) Hunt: rotate the specific secrets touched — cloud keys, SSH keys, browser sessions, Bitwarden vault, and AI-tool/MCP API keys — then sweep other hosts that installed jscrambler for the same acting-process pattern.

Persistence written by temp-dropped binary (hidden sched task / macOS LaunchAgent) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the stealer wiring in reboot persistence: a hidden Windows scheduled task set to relaunch every minute (schtasks /create ... minute) spawned from a temp-directory process, or a macOS LaunchAgent plist written into ~/Library/LaunchAgents by a process running from /tmp or /var/folders. Rationale: Anchors on the article's precise persistence detail — a hidden scheduled task set to relaunch every minute, and a macOS LaunchAgent reloading on login — combined with the parent being the temp-dropped binary. The Sentinel query now keys on 4688 NewProcessName + CommandLine instead of the non-existent TaskName column. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-backdoor-jscrambler-npm-package-with-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1543.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software installers creating per-minute health-check tasks from a temp-extracted setup binary
  • Monitoring agents (RMM tools) registering frequent scheduled tasks during deployment
  • macOS app installers dropping a LaunchAgent plist from a staged installer in /var/folders
  • An admin script creating a recurring task while logged in from an elevated temp-run tool
Suppression filter
| where not (ParentProcessName has_any ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe") and CommandLine has_any ("Adobe","Google","Microsoft"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the task action/target binary (schtasks /query /tn <name> /xml) or the LaunchAgent plist contents — a target pointing to a hidden temp file is confirmed malicious. 2) Contain: delete the scheduled task / remove the LaunchAgent plist, kill the referenced binary, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: search all jscrambler-affected hosts for per-minute tasks and unfamiliar ~/Library/LaunchAgents plists created since July 11, and correlate the task target hash against the UC2 payload hashes.
union
 (DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/create" and ProcessCommandLine has "minute" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Artifact = ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath),
 (DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/" and FileName endswith ".plist" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/folders/")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, Artifact = FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create" and CommandLine has "minute"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Hidden Per-Minute Scheduled Task Created from Temp Directory
id: d4a91f68-3b2c-4e70-9a15-6c8f2e1d7b39
description: Detects a per-minute scheduled task created by a temp-directory process, matching the jscrambler stealer Windows persistence

  parent_temp:

source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\schtasks.exe OR *\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:(*/create* OR */Create* OR */CREATE*) AND @CommandLine:*minute*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/schtasks\.exe$/i

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*" AND Processes.process="*minute*" AND (Processes.parent_process_path="*\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.parent_process_path="*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
jscrambler Package Tampering Artifact Detection AIDelivery Medium
Detects the tell-tale supply-chain artifacts of the compromise: the added dist/setup.js loader and dist/intro.js (a ~7.8MB binary container despite the .js name) appearing under node_modules/jscrambler, matched by the two published file hashes or by path+filename. These files exist in the npm tarball but nowhere in jscrambler's public source. Rationale: Uses the two published SHA-256 hashes for dist/setup.js and dist/intro.js plus the exact path/filename pattern (node_modules/jscrambler/dist). Multiple analysts (StepSecurity, SafeDep, Socket) confirmed these files exist in the tarball but not in the public repo, making their presence on disk high-fidelity supply-chain evidence. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-backdoor-jscrambler-npm-package-with-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated package or project that legitimately ships files named setup.js/intro.js in a directory containing 'jscrambler' in its path
  • A security researcher storing the extracted malicious files in a case folder path containing 'jscrambler'
  • A backup/restore operation replaying the tarball into a quarantined node_modules for analysis
  • A vendored copy of a clean older jscrambler release that happens to include a setup.js
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("\\case\\", "\\quarantine\\", "\\samples\\", "/analysis/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the on-disk setup.js/intro.js and compare to the published values; a match plus a ~7.8MB intro.js confirms the tampered package. 2) Contain: remove the node_modules/jscrambler tree and the lockfile pin, isolate the host if the preinstall hook already ran, and rebuild from a clean 8.13.0/8.15.0. 3) Hunt: search artifact registries, container images, and CI caches for these two hashes, then pivot to UC2/UC3 on any host where the files were present to confirm whether the payload executed.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60","a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86")
   or (FolderPath has "jscrambler" and FileName in~ ("setup.js","intro.js"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60","a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86")
   or (TargetFilePath has "jscrambler" and TargetFileName in~ ("setup.js","intro.js"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hackers Weaponize Balochistan Police Portal in Multi-Group Espionage Campaigns
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] cms_plugin.exe Rust stager execution + payload pull from 193.42.25.65 · [LLM] Fake 360Safe.exe (.NET) reflectively loading AsyncRAT · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Beaconing to Balochistan Police espionage C2 / stager IP set · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
cms_plugin.exe Rust stager execution + payload pull from 193.42.25.65 AIInstallation High
Hunts the custom 'cms_plugin.exe' implant that masqueraded as a Complaint Management System portal update on Balochistan Police infrastructure. The Rust stager variant downloads a next stage from 193.42.25.65 and prints 'Update Complete! Please refresh the page'. Fires on the named binary executing or any host reaching the stager download IP. Rationale: cms_plugin.exe is a unique implant filename and 193.42.25.65 is the confirmed Rust-stager download server named in the SentinelLABS report; both are non-generic, so a match is effectively a true positive. Cross-checked SentinelOne report and The Record write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://therecord.media/china-india-ran-separate-spy-campaigns-against-same-police-force
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-named plugin binary in an unrelated product also called cms_plugin.exe (rare; validate hash and path)
  • Security researcher / IR analyst detonating the sample in a sandbox VM enrolled in EDR
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliance actively probing 193.42.25.65 for research
  • Proxy/NAT egress IP collision where 193.42.25.65 is re-used by a benign CDN in future (validate at trigger time)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Sandbox\\" and DeviceName !in~ ("IR-SANDBOX-01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the process tree, SHA256, and folder path for cms_plugin.exe; confirm parent (likely w3wp.exe/web-app service on a CMS/web server) and whether the host is an internet-facing police web application server. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 193.42.25.65 at the perimeter, and preserve the binary for reversing. 3) Hunt: sweep all web servers for cms_plugin.exe uploads, search web logs on cms.balochistanpolice.gov.pk-style portals for the file, and pivot on the SHA1s and the full campaign C2 IP set (see C2 UC).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "193.42.25.65" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "cms_plugin.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where tolower(NewProcessName) endswith "\\cms_plugin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, Signal="process", NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Dest=""),
(CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "193.42.25.65"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer=SourceHostName, Account=SourceUserName, Signal="network", NewProcessName=ProcessName, CommandLine="", ParentProcessName="", Dest=DestinationIP)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Balochistan Police cms_plugin.exe Implant Execution
id: 6b1f2c9a-4d3e-4a11-9c77-2f0b8e5a1d42
description: Detects execution of the custom cms_plugin.exe implant deployed against Pakistani law enforcement (SentinelLABS).
references:
  - https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="cms_plugin.exe" OR Processes.original_file_name="cms_plugin.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_path Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="cms_plugin.exe" OR Processes.original_file_name="cms_plugin.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_path Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Fake 360Safe.exe (.NET) reflectively loading AsyncRAT AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the second cms_plugin.exe variant: a .NET executable that masquerades as '360Safe.exe' (a legitimate Qihoo 360 Total Security binary) to reflectively load an in-memory AsyncRAT client. Detects a process named 360Safe.exe whose file metadata is NOT Qihoo/360 or which runs from outside the legitimate 360 install path. Rationale: The report states one implant variant masquerades specifically as 360Safe.exe (Qihoo 360) to reflectively load AsyncRAT; a 360Safe.exe binary running outside the genuine Qihoo install path (or lacking Qihoo file metadata) is a high-fidelity masquerade signal, especially in a Pakistani gov environment unlikely to run Chinese AV. Corroborated by SentinelOne report and Kaspersky's Mysterious Elephant AsyncRAT/Remcos tradecraft. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://securelist.com/mysterious-elephant-apt-ttps-and-tools/117596/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Qihoo 360 Total Security installed to a non-default drive/path (validate publisher signature)
  • Portable/standalone 360 Total Security run from a USB or Downloads folder by a user
  • Software-deployment tool staging the real 360Safe.exe in a temp cache before install
  • AV bake-off / procurement testing of 360 Total Security by IT
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("360","Qihoo"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the digital signature and ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName of the 360Safe.exe image — genuine is signed by Qihoo/360; the implant will be unsigned or mis-signed. Inspect for .NET/CLR module loads and outbound connections. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture memory (AsyncRAT is in-memory), block associated C2 IPs. 3) Hunt: search DeviceImageLoadEvents for clr.dll/mscoree loading into 360Safe.exe, and correlate with cms_plugin.exe drops and the campaign C2 IP set.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "360Safe.exe"
| where not(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("360","Qihoo")) or FolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where tolower(NewProcessName) endswith "\\360safe.exe"
| where not(tolower(NewProcessName) startswith "c:\\program files (x86)\\360\\") and not(tolower(NewProcessName) startswith "c:\\program files\\360\\")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: Masquerading 360Safe.exe Outside Qihoo 360 Install Path
id: 8c2d4e17-9a55-4b3e-8f21-1d7c6b0e4a99
description: Detects a process named 360Safe.exe running from a non-standard path, consistent with the AsyncRAT loader used against Balochistan Police (SentinelLABS).
references:

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\360safe\.exe$/i

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="360Safe.exe" NOT (Processes.process_path="C:\\Program Files (x86)\\360\\*" OR Processes.process_path="C:\\Program Files\\360\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_path Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing to Balochistan Police espionage C2 / stager IP set AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound connections to the confirmed command-and-control and staging IPs across the four converging clusters (Cobalt Strike C2 142.171.183.8, Rust-stager host 193.42.25.65, plus the campaign infrastructure block) targeting Pakistani law enforcement. Any internal host reaching these IPs warrants investigation. Rationale: 142.171.183.8 is the named Cobalt Strike C2 and 193.42.25.65 the stager host; the remaining IPs are the pre-extracted campaign infrastructure. These are static, second-source-consistent IOCs, so egress to any of them is high-fidelity for this specific converging-actor campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://therecord.media/china-india-ran-separate-spy-campaigns-against-same-police-force
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An IOC IP later reassigned to a shared hosting/CDN provider serving benign sites (re-validate WHOIS at trigger time)
  • Internal threat-intel platform or vulnerability scanner actively probing the C2 IPs
  • Security researcher pivoting on the infrastructure from a corporate egress IP
  • Firewall/proxy that logs a blocked (denied) attempt — confirm DeviceAction/outcome is allow before escalating
Suppression filter
DeviceNetworkEvents | where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt") and RemoteIPType == "Public"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host and the InitiatingProcess making the connection; check whether the connection succeeded vs was blocked, and beacon regularity (jitter/interval). 2) Contain: block all listed IPs at the perimeter, isolate any host with a successful/repeated connection, and snapshot memory for the process (PlugX/ShadowPad/Cobalt Strike/AsyncRAT are memory-resident). 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiating process hash against the campaign SHA1 list, sweep for cms_plugin.exe and fake 360Safe.exe, and review the FortiMail email gateway and web-app servers for the initial foothold.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("142.171.183.8","193.42.25.65","41.216.188.140","89.31.121.220","45.125.32.218","172.111.233.36","172.111.233.96","172.111.233.12","172.111.233.105","172.111.233.26","172.94.9.49","172.94.9.43","172.94.9.19","45.74.6.17")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by LastSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("142.171.183.8","193.42.25.65","41.216.188.140","89.31.121.220","45.125.32.218","172.111.233.36","172.111.233.96","172.111.233.12","172.111.233.105","172.111.233.26","172.94.9.49","172.94.9.43","172.94.9.19","45.74.6.17")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(DestinationPort,10) by SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DeviceProduct
| order by LastSeen desc

id: 3f9a1c2b-7e64-4d0a-b3c1-9e2f5a8d7c10

references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/11
tags:

logsource:
  category: network_connection

detection:
  selection:

      - '142.171.183.8'
      - '193.42.25.65'
      - '41.216.188.140'
      - '89.31.121.220'
      - '45.125.32.218'
      - '172.111.233.36'
      - '172.111.233.96'
      - '172.111.233.12'
      - '172.111.233.105'
      - '172.111.233.26'

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationIp:(142.171.183.8 OR 193.42.25.65 OR 41.216.188.140 OR 89.31.121.220 OR 45.125.32.218 OR 172.111.233.36 OR 172.111.233.96 OR 172.111.233.12 OR 172.111.233.105 OR 172.111.233.26 OR 172.94.9.49 OR 172.94.9.43 OR 172.94.9.19 OR 45.74.6.17)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4=/^(142\.171\.183\.8|193\.42\.25\.65|41\.216\.188\.140|89\.31\.121\.220|45\.125\.32\.218|172\.111\.233\.(36|96|12|105|26)|172\.94\.9\.(49|43|19)|45\.74\.6\.17)$/
