XSS payload planted in SiYuan attribute-view storage (data/storage/av/*.json) by non-SiYuan process AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the persistence/plant step of CVE-2026-50551: the malicious cell lives in data/storage/av/<avID>.json and 'rides normal sync', so an attacker with write access to any synced workspace drops it once and it fires on every device that opens the panel. Flags writes to that exact path by a process other than SiYuan's own binaries (i.e. a third-party sync client, backup tool, git, or manual drop) — the delivery vector the advisory describes. Rationale: Uses the exact storage path from the advisory (data/storage/av/<avID>.json) plus the writer-identity discriminator: SiYuan's own kernel writes these constantly, so a third-party writer is the article's stated 'write access to any synced workspace' plant vector. Corroborated by GLAD CVE-2026-54158 confirming 'AV files live under the workspace and ride normal sync'. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-54158/ • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-56mp-4f3v-fgj2
ATT&CKT1080 T1565.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate third-party sync of the user's own edits (Syncthing.exe, OneDrive.exe, Dropbox.exe, GoogleDriveFS) writing the av JSON — same channel the attacker abuses
  • git.exe checkout/pull of a workspace kept under version control
  • Backup/restore tooling (Veeam, Duplicati, robocopy) writing av JSON during a restore
  • Manual copy of a workspace between machines via explorer.exe/xcopy
  • SiYuan running from a non-standard binary name in portable deployments
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("onedrive.exe","dropbox.exe","googledrivefs.exe","syncthing.exe") or FileName !endswith ".json"
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the flagged data/storage/av/*.json and search cell content for HTML breakout / handler strings ('</textarea>','">','<img','onerror=','onload=','javascript:'); identify the writing process and whether it is a sync/backup agent. 2) Contain: if payload strings are present, remove the poisoned row and pause sync for that workspace so it does not re-propagate; snapshot the file for IR. 3) Hunt: enumerate every device syncing the same workspace and check for SiYuan.exe child-process spawns (companion RCE UC) around and after the write time; confirm SiYuan is upgraded to >= 3.7.0 which escapes the text/url/phone/mAsset branches.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath has @"\data\storage\av\"
| where FileName endswith ".json"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("siyuan.exe","siyuan-kernel.exe","kernel.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\data\storage\av\"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".json"
| where ActingProcessName !has "siyuan"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File Browser hook-auth pre-auth RCE: filebrowser spawns shell/recon commands (CVE-2026-54088) AIExploitation High
Hunts the File Browser server binary (`filebrowser`) spawning a shell or OS discovery/tooling child process. Under CVE-2026-54088 an unauthenticated attacker injects shell metacharacters into the login username/password, which `os.Expand` substitutes unsanitised into the admin's hook-auth command, causing the `filebrowser` process to execute attacker OS commands. A file server should essentially never spawn `id`/`whoami`/`curl`/`wget`, so any such child is high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the concrete vulnerable binary name `filebrowser` (parent) plus the article's PoC injection primitive (shell metacharacters `;`/`$(`/backtick and `id`/`whoami` running under the hook command). A file-server process spawning recon/OS tooling is near-zero in benign operation. Cross-checked against filebrowser.org auth docs and auth/hook.go on GitHub. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m93h-4hw7-5qcm • https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/blob/master/auth/hook.go
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1033 T1087.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately configured a hook-auth command that shells out to an external auth backend using curl/wget (e.g. validating against an LDAP/OIDC gateway)
  • Custom container entrypoint or healthcheck wrapper also named 'filebrowser' spawning /bin/sh for readiness probes
  • Ops running the filebrowser CLI (`filebrowser config`, `filebrowser users`) interactively from a shell where the parent/child order is inverted
  • Backup/maintenance scripts invoked by a filebrowser-named systemd unit that call uname/hostname
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash") and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"^\s*test\s" and not (ProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the alert — confirm InitiatingProcessFileName=='filebrowser' and inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for injected recon (id/whoami/cat /etc/passwd) or separators; correlate to the host's web/reverse-proxy logs for a POST to /api/login in the same second. 2) Contain: isolate the host, stop the filebrowser container/service, and disable hook authentication (set auth.method back to json/proxy) or patch to filebrowser v2 > 2.63.5. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for follow-on egress/reverse shells (UC2), new files under the served directory (webshell/backdoor), new cron entries or SSH authorized_keys, and any outbound connection from the filebrowser process subtree.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "filebrowser"
| where (FileName in~ ("id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","python","python3","perl","ruby","php"))
    or (FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh","ksh")
        and (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","whoami","uname","/dev/tcp/")
             or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "filebrowser" or ParentProcessName has "filebrowser"
| where (TargetProcessName has_any ("/id","/whoami","/uname","/hostname","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/python","/perl","/ruby","/php"))
    or (TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/ash","/zsh","/ksh")
        and (TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","whoami","uname","/dev/tcp/")
             or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File Browser hook-auth RCE follow-on: reverse shell / egress tooling under filebrowser (CVE-2026-54088) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the File Browser process subtree spawning a reverse shell or ingress/download tool after successful command injection. Distinct from the discovery UC: this targets the C2 stage where the injected command establishes an interactive shell (`bash -i`, `/dev/tcp/`, `nc -e`, `socat`, `mkfifo`) or pulls a second-stage payload (`curl`/`wget` piped to a shell) from the `filebrowser` process. Rationale: Pairs the concrete vulnerable parent binary `filebrowser` with high-specificity reverse-shell/ingress signatures (`/dev/tcp/`, `bash -i`, `nc -e`, `socat`, `curl|wget` piped to shell) from the RCE class described in the advisory. These command-line strings are near-zero-FP and map the exploit to its C2/second-stage phase. Corroborated via filebrowser.org auth docs and the GHSA advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m93h-4hw7-5qcm • https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/blob/master/auth/hook.go
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105 T1571
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit hook-auth command that uses curl/wget to POST credentials to an external authentication API
  • filebrowser sidecar/init script that pulls config or TLS certs via curl/wget at startup
  • Admin debugging the container with `docker exec` where the shell's parent resolves to filebrowser
  • Monitoring agent invoking python from within the filebrowser service context for metrics
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("https://auth.","/certs/","/token") and ProcessCommandLine !has "/dev/tcp/" and ProcessCommandLine !has "| sh" and ProcessCommandLine !has "|sh")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the child ProcessCommandLine and resolve the destination host/port (grep for the IP after /dev/tcp/ or the nc/socat/curl target); check DeviceNetworkEvents on the same host for a matching outbound public connection in the same window. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the filebrowser process/container, block the observed C2 IP/domain at the egress firewall, and rotate any credentials/secrets readable by the filebrowser service account. 3) Hunt: search for downloaded second-stage files, persistence (cron, systemd units, authorized_keys), lateral SSH from this host, and repeat the UC1 discovery query to scope earlier recon.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "filebrowser"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh","ksh","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo","socat","import socket","import pty","curl ","wget ")
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bnc(\.traditional)?\b.*\s-[ec]\b"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "filebrowser" or ParentProcessName has "filebrowser"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/ash","/zsh","/ksh","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/curl","/wget","/python","/perl")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo","socat","import socket","import pty","curl ","wget ")
    or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bnc(\.traditional)?\b.*\s-[ec]\b"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FileBrowser proxy-auth bypass (CVE-2026-54089): direct inbound to app process bypassing reverse proxy AIDelivery Medium
Hunts direct network connections accepted by the FileBrowser (`filebrowser`) process from public/non-RFC1918 sources. In a correct proxy-auth deployment (auth.method=proxy) ALL traffic is fronted by nginx/Traefik/Caddy on loopback; any direct client reaching the app port can forge the X-Remote-User header for full admin takeover, so a direct inbound connection is the pre-condition for exploitation. Rationale: Anchors on the concrete `filebrowser` binary and the article's stated proxy-auth trust model (all traffic should arrive via loopback/proxy). A public-sourced inbound connection is the necessary pre-condition for the header-forgery bypass; cross-checked against GLAD advisory and FileBrowser Quantum proxy-auth docs. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/CVE-2026-54089/ • https://filebrowserquantum.com/en/docs/configuration/authentication/proxy/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Monitoring/uptime probes (Uptime-Kuma, Prometheus blackbox_exporter) hitting the exposed port from a monitoring host
  • Administrator accessing FileBrowser by IP:port directly for debugging, bypassing the proxy
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/OpenVAS) connecting to the port
  • Public load-balancer or Kubernetes kubelet liveness/health checks against the container port
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the RemoteIP — is it a known monitoring/LB/scanner asset or an unexpected external client? Check LocalPort matches the FileBrowser publish port and whether the host is meant to be proxy-fronted only. 2) Contain: if the source is untrusted, firewall the FileBrowser port to the reverse-proxy IP only (or rebind the container to 127.0.0.1), and rotate the JWT signing key to invalidate any minted admin tokens. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same SourceIP in web/proxy access logs for POST /api/login followed by /api/settings or /api/users (UC2/UC3), and review the FileBrowser user store for accounts created out-of-band.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "filebrowser"        // the FileBrowser Go binary
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"                          // proxy-auth setups should only see loopback/proxy
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 8085                            // FileBrowser published port (article PoC -p 8085:80)
| where DeviceAction in~ ("allow","permit","accept","") or isempty(DeviceAction)
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP)) and SourceIP != "127.0.0.1"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by LastSeen desc

FileBrowser CVE-2026-54089: forged X-Remote-User / X-Original-User header on /api/login AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP requests to FileBrowser's /api/login endpoint that carry a proxy-auth identity header (X-Remote-User / X-Original-User / Remote-User) sourced from the client rather than injected internally by the trusted proxy. FileBrowser unconditionally trusts this header to mint a JWT for any username (including admin) with no password check, so a client-supplied header on the login path is direct exploitation. Rationale: Uses the article's exact vulnerable endpoint (/api/login) and the trusted header name (X-Remote-User, per proxy.go and FileBrowser Quantum docs) plus the documented aliases. A client-set proxy-auth header on the login path is the literal exploit primitive; header capture at the proxy is the only place this value is visible (not in Defender/FDR endpoint tables). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/CVE-2026-54089/ • https://filebrowserquantum.com/en/docs/configuration/authentication/proxy/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The trusted reverse proxy's own hop legitimately injecting X-Remote-User (if the access log records post-injection headers on the loopback request)
  • Security scanners or authorized pentesters testing specifically for CVE-2026-54089
  • Internal tooling misconfigured to forward the identity header
  • Automated SSO integration test suites exercising the proxy-auth flow
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the request SourceIP is NOT the reverse-proxy address — a client-supplied X-Remote-User from any other IP is exploitation. Note the username value in the header (admin = full takeover). 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the proxy/WAF, rebind FileBrowser to loopback, and rotate the JWT signing key to revoke minted tokens; review the impacted account's actions. 3) Hunt: correlate the same SourceIP to subsequent /api/settings and /api/users calls (UC3), and search the user database for accounts auto-created from unknown usernames.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName in~ ("nginx","caddy","traefik","apache2","httpd")
| where SyslogMessage has "/api/login"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("X-Remote-User","X-Original-User","Remote-User")   // requires log_format that records the request header
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FileBrowser CVE-2026-54089: admin-endpoint access immediately after /api/login from same client (privilege jump) AIExploitation Medium
Correlates a FileBrowser /api/login request with admin-only API calls (/api/settings, /api/users, /api/resources with write/delete) from the same source IP within a 2-minute window. The proxy-auth bypass lets an unauthenticated client obtain an admin JWT in one request; a session that logs in and immediately performs admin actions with no legitimate elevation is the post-exploitation signature. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete admin endpoints (/api/settings, /api/users) reachable only by an admin JWT, correlated to the /api/login mint within a tight window. The temporal login->admin-action shape captures the credential-less privilege jump the CVE enables without needing header visibility, so it works on plain access logs. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/CVE-2026-54089/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm
ATT&CKT1548 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate administrator logging in then editing settings/users as part of normal workflow
  • Automation or IaC scripts that authenticate then provision users via the API
  • Backup or inventory tooling enumerating /api/resources shortly after auth
  • The reverse proxy's own health probe hitting /api/settings after a synthetic login
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the SourceIP is the reverse proxy (expected) or a direct external client (suspicious). Confirm the login used proxy-auth and identify the username/permission set that performed the admin action. 2) Contain: if the client is untrusted, block the IP, rebind FileBrowser to loopback, rotate the JWT signing key, and audit any settings/user changes made in the window. 3) Hunt: pivot on the SourceIP to UC1 (direct inbound) and UC2 (forged header), and diff the FileBrowser user store and settings against the last known-good backup for unauthorized changes.

    | where RequestURL has "/api/login"
    | project LoginTime = TimeGenerated, SourceIP, LoginURL = RequestURL;

| order by AdminActionTime desc

         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SiYuan: Unauthenticated Admin API Access via Blanket chrome-extension:// Origin Allowlist

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] SiYuan kernel listening on 6806 with empty AccessAuthCode (vulnerable exposure) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Non-browser process modifying Chrome/Edge extension files (CRX/manifest tampering)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Browser process connecting to SiYuan kernel admin API on 127.0.0.1:6806 · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Browser process connecting to SiYuan kernel admin API on 127.0.0.1:6806 AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for a Chrome/Chromium/Edge browser process opening a loopback connection to the SiYuan kernel HTTP server (port 6806). CVE-2026-54069 lets ANY installed extension reach this port and receive RoleAdministrator without a token, so browser-originated traffic to the kernel is the exploitation signal. Rationale: Uses the article's exact kernel endpoint (127.0.0.1:6806) plus the requirement that the caller is a browser rendering a chrome-extension:// origin. Corroborated by the GitLab advisory and SiYuan docs confirming 6806 as the default kernel port. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-54069/ • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan
ATT&CKT1176 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SiYuan's official web-clipper browser extension legitimately posting captured pages to 127.0.0.1:6806
  • User manually opening the SiYuan Web UI (http://127.0.0.1:6806) in a normal browser tab
  • Developer/power user testing the SiYuan API with browser dev-tools or a REST client extension
  • Browser-based automation or bookmarklet integrations the user deliberately installed
  • EDR loopback telemetry being sparse or absent on some agent versions (false negatives, not positives)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "siyuan" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "clipper"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the extension. Enumerate installed extensions on the host (Chrome ...\User Data\Default\Extensions) and compare the browser PID/command line to known-good; check whether the SiYuan official clipper is installed. 2) Contain: if the extension is unrecognized, remove it, force-close the browser, and set a non-empty AccessAuthCode on SiYuan; upgrade SiYuan to >=3.7.0. 3) Hunt: review SiYuan workspace for injected blocks (img onerror payloads), unexpected /api/system/setConf changes, and outbound connections from the SiYuan renderer to unfamiliar domains indicating stored-XSS beaconing.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 6806
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","chromium.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Conns=count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by FirstSeen desc

// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 6806
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","chromium.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Conns=count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Browser Process Connecting to SiYuan Kernel Admin Port 6806
id: 8f3a1c2e-5b7d-4e9a-9c11-2f6a0d4b7e10
description: Detects a Chromium-family browser opening a loopback connection to the SiYuan kernel HTTP server (CVE-2026-54069), the vector by which any extension gains unauthenticated RoleAdministrator.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hvr9-72v2-fff3
  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-54069/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/11
tags:
  - attack.t1176
  - attack.t1190
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\brave.exe'
      - '\chromium.exe'
      - '\opera.exe'
      - '\vivaldi.exe'
    DestinationPort: 6806
    DestinationIp:
      - '127.0.0.1'
      - '::1'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationPort:6806 (@DestinationIp:127.0.0.1 OR @DestinationIp:::1) @Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\msedge.exe OR *\\MsEdge.exe OR *\\brave.exe OR *\\chromium.exe OR *\\opera.exe OR *\\vivaldi.exe)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort=6806
| RemoteAddressIP4=/^127\.0\.0\.1$/
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|brave|chromium|opera|vivaldi)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=6806 (All_Traffic.dest="127.0.0.1" OR All_Traffic.dest="::1") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | eval proc=lower(coalesce(process_name,app)) | where like(proc,"%chrome%") OR like(proc,"%msedge%") OR like(proc,"%brave%") OR like(proc,"%chromium%") OR like(proc,"%opera%") OR like(proc,"%vivaldi%") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=6806 (All_Traffic.dest="127.0.0.1" OR All_Traffic.dest="::1") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | eval proc=lower(coalesce(process_name,app)) | where like(proc,"%chrome%") OR like(proc,"%msedge%") OR like(proc,"%brave%") OR like(proc,"%chromium%") OR like(proc,"%opera%") OR like(proc,"%vivaldi%") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
SiYuan kernel listening on 6806 with empty AccessAuthCode (vulnerable exposure) AIReconnaissance Medium
Exposure hunt that surfaces hosts where the SiYuan kernel (siyuan.exe) is listening on TCP 6806, projecting the product version so an analyst can flag installs <= 3.6.5 that predate the CVE-2026-54069 fix (3.7.0). Confirms which endpoints are actually exploitable by the chrome-extension origin bypass. Rationale: Anchors on siyuan.exe + the article's named default kernel port 6806 and projects InitiatingProcessVersionInfoProductVersion so the analyst can gate on <=3.6.5 vs the corroborated fixed version 3.7.0. Sentinel left empty: listener/port-bind attribution to a process is not available in standard Sentinel tables (needs Sysmon EID3 or Defender XDR). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-54069/ • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan
ATT&CKT1190 T1518
Data sourcesEndpoint.Ports
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SiYuan installs already upgraded to >=3.7.0 (patched) still listening on 6806 — check the projected version
  • Users who set a non-empty AccessAuthCode (not exploitable even if listening) — version/port alone can't see the auth config
  • Docker/self-hosted SiYuan bound intentionally on a locked-down host
  • Non-SiYuan software coincidentally bound to 6806 (excluded by the siyuan process filter)
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, read InitiatingProcessVersionInfoProductVersion; versions <=3.6.5 are vulnerable. Confirm whether AccessAuthCode is set (SiYuan Settings > About / conf.json). 2) Contain: push SiYuan >=3.7.0 to affected hosts and enforce a non-empty AccessAuthCode via SIYUAN_ACCESS_AUTH_CODE. 3) Hunt: on any host that was vulnerable, run the browser->6806 detection retrospectively to see if exploitation occurred, and review notes for injected content.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ListeningConnectionCreated"
| where LocalPort == 6806
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "siyuan"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessVersionInfoProductVersion, LocalIP, LocalPort
| order by FirstSeen desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.

// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ListeningConnectionCreated"
| where LocalPort == 6806
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "siyuan"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessVersionInfoProductVersion, LocalIP, LocalPort
| order by FirstSeen desc
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\siyuan\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, FileVersion], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Ports where Ports.dest_port=6806 Ports.transport=tcp by Ports.dest Ports.dest_port Ports.process_name Ports.transport | `drop_dm_object_name(Ports)` | where like(lower(process_name),"%siyuan%") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Ports where Ports.dest_port=6806 Ports.transport=tcp by Ports.dest Ports.dest_port Ports.process_name Ports.transport | `drop_dm_object_name(Ports)` | where like(lower(process_name),"%siyuan%") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Non-browser process modifying Chrome/Edge extension files (CRX/manifest tampering) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the supply-chain amplification path called out in the advisory: a non-browser process writing manifest.json, .crx, or background scripts into a Chromium extension directory. A tampered/backdoored extension is what silently exploits every SiYuan desktop user via CVE-2026-54069. Rationale: Grounded in the advisory's 'compromised legitimate extension via supply chain attack' / 'single compromised popular Chrome extension update can silently exploit every SiYuan desktop user' claim; the high-fidelity twist is a NON-browser process writing extension payload files, which normal Chrome/Edge auto-updates never do. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-54069/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise extension deployment via GPO/Intune or a management agent writing force-installed extensions
  • Manual developer 'load unpacked' workflow copying files into a profile Extensions folder
  • Backup/sync software (OneDrive, Dropbox) touching profile files inside the browser directory
  • Security tooling that unpacks/inspects .crx files in place
  • Portable-browser launchers seeding an extension set on first run
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "Intune" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("onedrive.exe","dropbox.exe","backup.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process and the target extension ID; hash the modified manifest.json/background script and diff against the Web Store version. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, quarantine the extension folder, block the writing process, and disable the extension in the browser policy. 3) Hunt: check the same host for browser->127.0.0.1:6806 connections (SiYuan exploitation) and review SiYuan notes/config for injected blocks or setConf tampering; sweep the fleet for the same extension ID and writer hash.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data", @"\Chromium\User Data", @"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data")
| where FolderPath has @"\Extensions\"
| where FileName =~ "manifest.json" or FileName endswith ".crx" or FileName endswith ".js"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","chromium.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","googleupdate.exe","update.exe","microsoftedgeupdate.exe","elevation_service.exe","msiexec.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data", @"\Chromium\User Data", @"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Extensions\"
| where TargetFileName =~ "manifest.json" or TargetFileName endswith ".crx" or TargetFileName endswith ".js"
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","chromium.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","googleupdate.exe","microsoftedgeupdate.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 4d21e9b7-6a3c-4f18-8e52-91b7c0a3d5f2
description: Detects manifest.json/.crx/.js writes inside a Chromium-family extension folder by a process that is not the browser or its updater, indicating extension tampering (CVE-2026-54069 supply-chain vector).
references:

| regex("\\\\User Data\\\\.*\\\\Extensions\\\\", field=TargetFileName)
| TargetFileName=/(manifest\.json|\.crx|\.js)$/i
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|brave|chromium|GoogleUpdate|MicrosoftEdgeUpdate|elevation_service)\.exe$/i)

Authorizer /authorize implicit-flow request with off-app redirect_uri (CVE-2026-54072) AIExploitation High
Hunts the exploit request for CVE-2026-54072: a GET to Authorizer's /authorize endpoint using response_type=token or response_type=id_token (implicit/hybrid flow) that carries a redirect_uri to an absolute external URL. Authorizer never validates redirect_uri against AllowedOrigins on this handler, so the server 302-redirects the victim's access_token/id_token/refresh_token to the attacker host. Article-specific because it keys on the exact endpoint, response_type values, and redirect_uri shape from the PoC. Rationale: Keys on the article's exact PoC strings: endpoint /authorize, response_type=token / id_token, and an absolute redirect_uri — legitimate Authorizer clients use the authorization-code flow (response_type=code), so implicit-flow requests carrying an off-app redirect_uri are inherently rare and high-fidelity. Cross-checked GHSA-h29v-hj44-q8cv and the GitLab/GHSA-x3f4-v83f-7wp2 sibling advisory (CWE-601). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/authorizerdev/authorizer/CVE-2026-54072/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x3f4-v83f-7wp2
ATT&CKT1190 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate SPA still using the OAuth2 implicit flow (response_type=token) against a registered AllowedOrigin
  • Security scanners / penetration testers replaying the CVE PoC during authorized assessment
  • Internal QA or staging redirect_uri pointing at localhost/127.0.0.1 during development
  • Mobile/native app using a custom-scheme or loopback redirect that is legitimately registered
Suppression filter
| where Url !has_any ("redirect_uri=http://localhost", "redirect_uri=http%3A%2F%2Flocalhost", "redirect_uri=http://127.0.0.1", "redirect_uri=http%3A%2F%2F127.0.0.1")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the redirect_uri host from the flagged Url and compare it to the tenant's configured AllowedOrigins; if it is an unrecognized external domain, treat as active exploitation. Note SrcIpAddr and the HttpStatusCode (302 = tokens were issued). 2) Contain: block the attacker redirect host at proxy/WAF, and upgrade Authorizer to >= 0.0.0-20260409051328-bd3f5baf6d3d which adds IsValidOrigin() to authorize.go; force token/session revocation for any user whose session hit the endpoint. 3) Hunt: pivot on SrcIpAddr for prior POST /graphql (client_id recon) and for any outbound request carrying access_token= in its URL (exfiltration UC).
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/authorize"
| where Url has_any ("response_type=token", "response_type=id_token")   // implicit/hybrid flow returns tokens in the redirect
| where Url has "redirect_uri="
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)redirect_uri=https?(:|%3A)"          // absolute off-app redirect target
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OAuth tokens (access_token/id_token/refresh_token) in outbound URL to external host (CVE-2026-54072 exfiltration) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the exfiltration step of CVE-2026-54072: after Authorizer 302-redirects to the attacker URL, the victim browser (or proxy) issues a request whose query string carries access_token together with id_token/refresh_token/token_type=bearer. OAuth tokens should never appear in a URL query string on the wire, so this is the smoking-gun signal the reviewer flagged. Article-specific because it matches the exact parameter names the server appends to redirect_uri. Rationale: Uses the exact token parameter names (access_token, id_token, refresh_token, token_type=bearer) the article says the server appends to redirect_uri; tokens in a URL query string are a near-zero-baseline artifact, making this alerting-grade regardless of the attacker's specific domain. Not shippable to Defender/Falcon (host EDR does not carry full URL query strings over TLS). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h29v-hj44-q8cv • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/authorizerdev/authorizer/CVE-2026-54072/
ATT&CKT1567 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A poorly designed legacy SSO/callback endpoint that legitimately passes access_token in the query string rather than the URL fragment
  • Debug/verbose logging that echoes a token-bearing URL into an access log for an internal test client
  • Automated OAuth conformance tests exercising the implicit flow in a lab tenant
  • A security scanner replaying the CVE PoC during an authorized test
Response runbook
1) Triage: read DstHostname — if it is not a first-party SSO/callback host, the token bundle has left the org; capture the token values' subject by decoding the id_token JWT to identify the victim account. 2) Contain: revoke the leaked access_token/refresh_token and terminate the victim's Authorizer sessions; block DstHostname at proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: search authentication and API logs for use of the leaked token (impersonation) after the leak time, and correlate SrcIpAddr/victim with the /authorize exploit UC to confirm the full chain.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "access_token="
| where Url has_any ("id_token=", "refresh_token=", "token_type=bearer")   // full OAuth bundle in the URL = leaked, not normal
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderReferer, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Authorizer client_id recon via /graphql followed by implicit-flow /authorize (CVE-2026-54072) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the reconnaissance-to-exploit pivot for CVE-2026-54072: the same source issues a POST to Authorizer's public /graphql endpoint (used to read {meta{client_id}} without authentication) and then, within 10 minutes, a /authorize request using response_type=token/id_token. Correlating the two endpoints from one source captures the attacker learning the required client_id and immediately weaponizing it, which neither event alone reveals. Rationale: Chains the two article-named endpoints (/graphql for unauthenticated client_id disclosure, /authorize for the implicit-flow exploit) from a single SrcIpAddr inside a tight window; GraphQL bodies are POST payloads not present in access logs, so the endpoint sequence is the strongest available recon signal. Skipped Sigma because this is a cross-event temporal correlation, not a single-event shape. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h29v-hj44-q8cv
ATT&CKT1595 T1592.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate SPA that reads {meta{client_id}} on load and then starts an implicit-flow login for a real user, from the same NAT/egress IP
  • Corporate proxy that collapses many users behind one SrcIpAddr, making /graphql and /authorize appear co-sourced
  • Uptime/synthetic monitoring that probes both endpoints in sequence
  • Authorized vulnerability scan walking the OAuth endpoints
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the /authorize leg uses response_type=token with an off-app redirect_uri (benign SPAs use response_type=code); if so the recon->exploit chain is real. Check whether SrcIpAddr is a shared corporate egress before escalating. 2) Contain: block the source and the attacker redirect host at the WAF; patch Authorizer to the fixed pseudo-version. 3) Hunt: from the same SrcIpAddr pivot to any outbound URL carrying access_token= (exfiltration UC), and review /graphql volume from that source for broader introspection sweeps.
let win = 10m;
let recon = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Url has "/graphql"
    | where HttpMethod == "POST"                       // unauthenticated {meta{client_id}} probe is a POST
    | project ReconTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, ReconUrl = Url;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/authorize"
| where Url has_any ("response_type=token", "response_type=id_token")
| project AuthTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, AuthUrl = Url, DstHostname
| join kind=inner recon on SrcIpAddr
| where AuthTime between (ReconTime .. ReconTime + win)
| project SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, ReconTime, AuthTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', AuthTime, ReconTime), ReconUrl, AuthUrl
| order by AuthTime desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.uri_path="/graphql" OR Web.uri_path="/authorize") by _time span=1s Web.src Web.uri_path Web.uri_query Web.http_method
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval phase=case(uri_path=="/graphql" AND http_method=="POST","recon", uri_path=="/authorize" AND (like(uri_query,"%response_type=token%") OR like(uri_query,"%response_type=id_token%")),"exploit", true(),null())
| where isnotnull(phase)
| sort 0 src _time
| streamstats current=f last(_time) as prevTime last(phase) as prevPhase by src
| where phase=="exploit" AND prevPhase=="recon" AND (_time - prevTime) <= 600
| eval DelaySec=(_time - prevTime)
| table _time src DelaySec uri_path uri_query
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.uri_path="/graphql" OR Web.uri_path="/authorize") by _time span=1s Web.src Web.uri_path Web.uri_query Web.http_method
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
SiYuan Electron renderer (nodeIntegration) spawning shell/LOLBin child — XSS-to-RCE AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE stage of CVE-2026-54067 (and the sibling SiYuan XSS-to-RCE bugs): a stored snippet/caption/README breaks out of its HTML context and, because the renderer runs with nodeIntegration:true, calls require('child_process') to spawn a command interpreter. A Markdown note app should essentially never parent cmd.exe/powershell.exe, so this parent->child pair is high-fidelity across the whole SiYuan RCE bug class. Rationale: Anchored on InitiatingProcessFileName=siyuan.exe (the Electron main/renderer binary confirmed in the advisory as running nodeIntegration:true/contextIsolation:false) parenting a command interpreter — the observable end state of require('child_process').execSync from injected JS. Node's execSync on Windows spawns cmd.exe, making cmd.exe the highest-value child. Robust across all SiYuan XSS-to-RCE variants. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-phhp-9rm9-6gr2 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-44670/ • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-54067
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SiYuan document export to PDF/Word invoking a bundled pandoc/wkhtmltopdf helper (verify child binary is the export helper, not a shell)
  • User-configured 'open with' / external-command plugins in SiYuan that legitimately shell out
  • A power-user snippet the owner wrote themselves that intentionally calls a benign command (confirm with the user)
  • SiYuan auto-update or crash-reporter helper launched via cmd.exe wrapper
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("pandoc", "wkhtmltopdf", "--export", "SiYuan-Kernel"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the child ProcessCommandLine and SHA256 — a benign export helper looks nothing like a shell one-liner. Check whether the same user recently edited a CSS/JS snippet or synced a workspace. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the child process tree, and revoke/rotate any SiYuan Cloud / S3 / WebDAV sync credentials for that workspace so the poisoned snippet can't re-propagate. 3) HUNT: Retrieve data/snippets/conf.json from every peer that syncs the same workspace and grep for '</style>' or 'onerror='; upgrade all SiYuan clients to >=3.7.0; sweep other hosts for siyuan.exe parenting interpreters over the last 30 days.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "siyuan.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","calc.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\siyuan.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\curl.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\calc.exe")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Non-SiYuan process writing synced snippet store data\snippets\conf.json AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the plant/delivery stage of CVE-2026-54067: the malicious CSS snippet is stored in the workspace file data/snippets/conf.json, which syncs to every peer. When a process OTHER than the SiYuan kernel writes that file — e.g. a Dropbox/Syncthing/Google Drive sync client, a text editor, or a shared-drive process — it indicates the snippet store was tampered with out-of-band, exactly the 'workspace-write compromise via shared filesystem' vector the advisory calls out. Rationale: Uses the exact storage path from the advisory (data/snippets/conf.json, referenced at kernel/model/repository.go:1748,1798) and excludes the legitimate writer (the SiYuan kernel). A write by a sync client or editor is the out-of-band tamper path the advisory enumerates (Dropbox/Syncthing/network share/git). Cross-checked against: • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-54067 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-44670/
ATT&CKT1080 T1195
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dropbox.exe / SyncthingTray.exe / googledrivefs.exe legitimately syncing a workspace whose owner edited snippets on another device (benign but the exact tamper vector — inspect the resulting content)
  • A backup agent (Veeam, Duplicati, Acronis) reading/rewriting the workspace folder
  • User editing conf.json directly in VS Code / Notepad++ during troubleshooting
  • Git client (git.exe) pulling a workspace tracked in version control
  • Antivirus/EDR quarantine-and-restore touching the file
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","duplicati.exe","backup.exe") and InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "git.exe"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Open the written data/snippets/conf.json and grep for '</style>', 'onerror=', '<img', or 'child_process' — a benign sync writes normal CSS/JS. Note the writing process and account. 2) CONTAIN: If payload strings are present, quarantine the workspace, block sync (pause Dropbox/Syncthing, revoke WebDAV/S3 creds), and prevent SiYuan from loading the poisoned snippet until cleaned. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every device syncing the same workspace and check for the same conf.json write; pivot to UC #1 (siyuan.exe spawning a shell) on those hosts to see if RCE already fired; confirm all clients are >=3.7.0.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\data\snippets\" and FileName =~ "conf.json"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("siyuan.exe","siyuan-kernel.exe","kernel.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\data\snippets\" and TargetFileName =~ "conf.json"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where not(ActingProcessName has "siyuan")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ShareFile Storage Zone Controller pre-auth exploit URIs in IIS logs (CVE-2026-2699/2701) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the specific ShareFile Storage Zone Controller endpoints abused in the watchTowr-disclosed pre-auth RCE chain: the ConfigService auth-bypass page, the misspelled StroageZoneConfig API, and upload.aspx with an unzip parameter. This is the exact initial-access signature behind Progress's shutdown order. Rationale: Uses the exact exploit endpoints from watchTowr's chain writeup — /ConfigService/Admin.aspx (auth bypass), the misspelled /ConfigService/api/StroageZoneConfig, and upload.aspx?...unzip. The typo'd internal API path is effectively pathognomonic for exploitation. IIS logs are the only telemetry carrying the URI, so Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch are left empty. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/youre-not-supposed-to-sharefile-with-everyone-progress-sharefile-pre-auth-rce-chain-cve-2026-2699-cve-2026-2701/ • https://watchtowr.com/resources/progress-sharefile-storage-zone-controller-pre-auth-rce-cve-2026-2699-cve-2026-2701/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/progress-urges-sharefile-customers-to-shut-down-servers-over-credible-threat/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Qualys/Tenable/Rapid7) probing the same endpoints
  • watchTowr / Shadowserver internet-wide exposure scans hitting /ConfigService
  • Legitimate ShareFile admin reaching /ConfigService/Admin.aspx from an internal management IP after authenticating
  • Security team replaying PoC during authorized IR validation
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("<internal_vuln_scanner_ip>") // suppress authorized scanner ranges; keep external IPs in scope
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all hits for the offending cIP; check scStatus — a 200/302 on /ConfigService/Admin.aspx or a POST to upload.aspx?...unzip from an external IP is a likely successful exploit, and requests to the misspelled StroageZoneConfig confirm PoC-derived tooling. 2) Contain: per Progress guidance, keep the controller offline; block the source IP at the perimeter and preserve IIS logs and the storage tree for forensics. 3) Hunt: on the same host pivot to newly written .aspx files under \StorageCenter\ (UC2) and w3wp.exe child shells (UC3); scope the source IP across all internet-facing assets.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csUriStem has_any ("/ConfigService/Admin.aspx", "/ConfigService/api/StroageZoneConfig", "/documentum/upload.aspx")
   or (csUriStem endswith "/upload.aspx" and csUriQuery has "unzip")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SrcIP = cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, UserAgent = csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ShareFile Storage Zone Controller IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawns shell/recon child AIInstallation High
Detects the post-exploitation execution stage of the ShareFile pre-auth RCE: the IIS worker process hosting the Storage Zone Controller (w3wp.exe) spawning interactive shells or host-recon binaries, which is how an uploaded ASPX webshell runs commands. Directly supports the article's 'treat it as a possible incident' guidance. Rationale: w3wp.exe (the IIS worker) spawning cmd/powershell/recon binaries is the direct execution artifact of an ASPX webshell running commands on the Storage Zone Controller — the exact chain outcome watchTowr demonstrated. Parent=w3wp + child shell/LOLBin is the high-fidelity pair; scope to ShareFile SZC hosts via the FP filter to cut other IIS app pools. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/youre-not-supposed-to-sharefile-with-everyone-progress-sharefile-pre-auth-rce-chain-cve-2026-2699-cve-2026-2701/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2023/08/17/cve-2023-24489-exploited/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/progress-sharefile-admins-shut-down-servers/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Other IIS-hosted web apps on the same server legitimately shelling out (custom .NET apps calling Process.Start)
  • Web app deployment/maintenance running appcmd, DISM, or provisioning scripts under w3wp
  • Monitoring/APM agents invoking cmd or PowerShell from the worker
  • Admin troubleshooting an app pool via a diagnostic .aspx page
  • Backup or config tooling that shells out during app-pool recycle
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("StorageCenter", "documentum", "ShareFile") // restrict to the ShareFile SZC app pool; drop to widen to all IIS
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect ProcessCommandLine of the child — whoami/net/nltest recon or download strings (certutil/bitsadmin/curl) launched by w3wp on a ShareFile host is near-certain webshell RCE; capture the full process tree and parent w3wp command line (app-pool name). 2) Contain: isolate the host and keep the controller offline per Progress guidance; snapshot memory before reboot to preserve any in-memory implant. 3) Hunt: correlate to newly written .aspx under \StorageCenter\ (UC3) and inbound exploit URIs (UC1) within the preceding minutes; sweep for outbound connections from w3wp and new local accounts/services.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","ipconfig.exe","systeminfo.exe","nltest.exe","hostname.exe","tasklist.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","reg.exe","sc.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\cmd.exe", @"\powershell.exe", @"\pwsh.exe", @"\net.exe", @"\net1.exe", @"\whoami.exe", @"\ipconfig.exe", @"\systeminfo.exe", @"\nltest.exe", @"\hostname.exe", @"\tasklist.exe", @"\cscript.exe", @"\wscript.exe", @"\certutil.exe", @"\bitsadmin.exe", @"\reg.exe", @"\sc.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ASPX webshell written under ShareFile Storage Zone Controller storage path AIInstallation High
Detects creation of ASPX/ASHX web-executable files inside the Storage Zone Controller's IIS-served storage tree (…\StorageCenter\…\files\ul-…), which is where the CVE-2026-2699/2701 chain drops its webshell. This is the persistence artifact Progress told admins to look for ('unfamiliar .aspx files in the web folders and storage paths'). Rationale: watchTowr confirmed the webshell lands under the SZC storage location that overlaps the IIS web root (e.g. C:\inetpub\wwwroot\ShareFile\StorageCenter\documentum\files\ul-<id>\1\). A newly created .aspx/.ashx under any \StorageCenter\ path is the article's 'unfamiliar .aspx' artifact — legitimate ShareFile user uploads are documents, not server-executable pages in that tree. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/youre-not-supposed-to-sharefile-with-everyone-progress-sharefile-pre-auth-rce-chain-cve-2026-2699-cve-2026-2701/ • https://support.sharefile.com/s/article/ShareFile-StorageZones-Controller-Security-Update-for-CVE-2023-24489 • https://docs.sharefile.com/en-us/storage-zones-controller/5-0/security-vulnerability-feb26.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Progress-signed installer/upgrade writing legitimate .aspx pages during a 5.12.4 patch deployment
  • Admin manually placing a diagnostic or health-check .aspx in the StorageCenter web app
  • A user legitimately uploading a document literally named *.aspx into a ShareFile storage zone (rare)
  • Backup/restore tooling re-creating the StorageCenter directory tree
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe", "ShareFile.StorageCenter.Setup.exe", "TrustedInstaller.exe") // exclude signed installer/patch writes; investigate w3wp.exe-authored files
Response runbook
1) Triage: retrieve and read the file contents/hash — webshell indicators are eval/Request/Process.Start/cmd handlers; check InitiatingProcess (w3wp.exe writing it is damning) and creation time against the patch-deployment window. 2) Contain: keep the controller offline per Progress; quarantine the file, preserve a copy for forensics, and block the uploading source IP. 3) Hunt: pivot to inbound exploit URIs (UC1) and w3wp child shells (UC2) near the file-creation time; hash-sweep all SZC hosts for the same file and scan every internet-facing controller for .aspx under \StorageCenter\.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has @"\StorageCenter\"
| where FileName endswith ".aspx" or FileName endswith ".ashx" or FileName endswith ".asmx" or FileName endswith ".asp"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\StorageCenter\"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("aspx", "ashx", "asmx", "asp")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-2699", "CVE-2026-2701", "CVE-2023-24489")

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-2699", "CVE-2026-2701", "CVE-2023-24489")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Injective Labs GitHub Compromise Pushes Wallet-Key-Stealing npm Packages

The Hacker News
2026-07-10 13 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Unknown threat actors compromised the Injective Labs SDK project's GitHub repository and leveraged it to publish a malicious package on the npm registry to steal cryptocurrency wallet private keys and mnemonic seed phrases. The compromised version, @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21, came embedded with fake telemetry functionality that exfiltrated data from cryptocurrency wallets. The version was

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Install/pin of malicious @injectivelabs ...@1.20.21 supply-chain version in package manager cmdline
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Trojanized @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.21 artifact by SHA256 on developer/CI endpoints · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Wallet-key exfil beacon to Injective SDK C2 host testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Wallet-key exfil beacon to Injective SDK C2 host testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound DNS/HTTPS to the exact attacker subdomain that the trojanized @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 uses to POST stolen private keys and mnemonics. The host is shaped to blend with real Injective gRPC-web infra but this specific FQDN is attacker-controlled and appears only in the malicious build. Rationale: The FQDN testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network is the single hard-coded exfil endpoint confirmed by Socket, Aikido and OX Security; it never appears in legitimate Injective SDK traffic, making an exact-match resolution/connection a near-zero-FP signal. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/compromised-injective-sdk-npm-package • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-injectivelabs-exfiltrates-keys • https://www.ox.security/blog/injectivelabs-npm-package-hijacked-impacting-87-dependent-packages/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/injective-sdk-on-npm-infected-with-cryptocurrency-wallet-stealer/
ATT&CKT1041 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment/sandbox tooling actively resolving the IOC for validation
  • SOAR/EDR auto-detonation of the flagged package in a lab detonation host
  • Security researcher reproducing the attack in an isolated build
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ appliance logging the blocked lookup
  • Passive-DNS collector replaying historical resolutions
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sandbox_detonator.exe","threatintel-resolver.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/user and the process that opened the connection (Node.js/CI runner) and confirm @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.21 is present in that project's node_modules/lockfile. 2) Contain: block the FQDN at DNS/proxy, isolate the developer/CI host, and treat every private key or mnemonic ever handled on that host as compromised — force wallet key/seed rotation immediately. 3) Hunt: pivot on the two malicious artifact SHA256s across all endpoints and CI, enumerate all 18 pinned @injectivelabs@1.20.21 packages and transitive dependents, and search for prior beacons to the host over the full retention window.

Trojanized @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.21 artifact by SHA256 on developer/CI endpoints AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the on-disk presence of the two known-malicious release artifacts of the compromised Injective SDK build, which remained downloadable from GitHub even after npm deprecation. High-fidelity because it keys on published file hashes, not behavior. Rationale: Keys on the two SHA256 artifact hashes published for the compromised build (still hosted on GitHub after npm deprecation); a file-hash match is deterministic and requires no behavioral inference. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/compromised-injective-sdk-npm-package • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-injectivelabs-exfiltrates-keys
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis/repro workstation intentionally holding the sample
  • EDR quarantine or forensic evidence store retaining the file
  • Security team distributing the IOC bundle internally for testing
  • Backup/snapshot restore surfacing an old node_modules copy
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "\\Quarantine\\" and FolderPath !has "\\malware-samples\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the hash hit is within a live project (node_modules/cache) versus a quarantine/analysis path, and identify the owning developer/CI job. 2) Contain: remove/upgrade to clean @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.23, purge npm caches, and rotate every wallet private key/mnemonic that transited that host. 3) Hunt: enumerate all 18 @injectivelabs@1.20.21 pinned packages and transitive dependents in lockfiles org-wide, and correlate with any beacon to testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network.

Install/pin of malicious @injectivelabs ...@1.20.21 supply-chain version in package manager cmdline AIDelivery Medium
Hunts npm/yarn/pnpm invocations that install or pin the poisoned 1.20.21 version of the Injective SDK or its 17 sibling wallet packages, catching the compromise at install time even when the artifact hash has been rebuilt. Article-specific to the exact malicious version string and scoped package names. Rationale: Combines the scoped package prefix @injectivelabs/ with the exact malicious version 1.20.21 (Socket/OX Security list all 18 packages pinned to that version); the clean release is 1.20.23, so a 1.20.21 pin in a package-manager cmdline is a strong install-time indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ox.security/blog/injectivelabs-npm-package-hijacked-impacting-87-dependent-packages/ • https://socket.dev/blog/compromised-injective-sdk-npm-package
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer intentionally pinning 1.20.21 for repro/forensics before remediation
  • CI pipeline replaying an old lockfile that still references 1.20.21
  • Dependency-scanning tool echoing the version string in its own command line
  • Internal advisory script that greps for the bad version by name
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "dependency-scan" and ProcessCommandLine !has "--dry-run"
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the command actually installed (exit success, node_modules populated) versus a scan/echo, and identify the repo and user. 2) Contain: bump the dependency to 1.20.23 across affected repos, invalidate CI caches, and rotate any wallet secrets exercised on that runner/host. 3) Hunt: sweep all lockfiles/package.json for @injectivelabs@1.20.21 and transitive pins, then correlate hosts with the C2-domain and artifact-hash detections.

| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "@injectivelabs/" and ProcessCommandLine has "1.20.21"
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm","yarn","pnpm")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

SecurityEvent

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.

| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")

          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:

            - '\Cookies'

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName

SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
